package_info.package_manager: N/A (delivered via email attachment, not a package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: The HTML file is crafted to exploit the Windows Search URI protocol, redirecting users to a remote malicious server via search queries. This enables the attacker to execute unauthorized code, deliver malware payloads, and exfiltrate data by abusing Windows Search and WebDAV, all under the guise of a legitimate document.

execution_context.trigger: user interaction (opening HTML attachment in email)
execution_context.file_location: malicious HTML file inside zipped email attachment

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon opening the HTML file, the browser immediately redirects to a Windows Search URI, triggering Windows Explorer to perform a search for files named 'INVOICE' in a specified location, with the display name set to 'Downloads'.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: HTML files should not trigger OS-level search operations or redirect to custom URI schemes that interact with the local file system.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal HTML documents are not expected to invoke Windows Search or interact with the file system via custom URI schemes.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some enterprise environments may use custom URI schemes for internal tools, but not for unsolicited email attachments.
key_indicators: Use of <meta http-equiv="refresh"> for instant redirection
Targeting of specific file names to lure users

execution_context.trigger: user interaction (clicking a link in the HTML file)
execution_context.file_location: malicious HTML file inside zipped email attachment

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user clicks the link, Windows Explorer is triggered to perform a search for 'INVOICE' files, but the search location is a remote WebDAV share controlled by the attacker, making malicious files appear as local resources.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: HTML links should not invoke Windows Search on remote shares, especially those tunneled through services like Cloudflare.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal HTML links are expected to point to web resources, not to local or remote file system searches via OS-level protocols.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Internal documentation may use search-ms: links for productivity, but not in unsolicited email attachments.
key_indicators: search-ms: URI with remote UNC path
Display name set to mimic legitimate folders
Encouragement to click via social engineering

execution_context.file_location: Windows Registry (via command line or script)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After exploitation, the attacker removes the Windows Search URI protocol handler from the registry to prevent further detection or use.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Deleting protocol handlers from the registry is a strong indicator of anti-forensic or persistence techniques.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software rarely removes protocol handlers without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System administrators may remove unused protocols for hardening, but not as part of document handling.
key_indicators: Use of /f flag for forced deletion

attack_chain.action: User receives a phishing email with a zipped HTML attachment.
HTML file executes a meta refresh or presents a clickable link that triggers the Windows Search URI protocol.
attack_chain.leads_to: Windows Explorer performs a search, potentially accessing remote malicious files.

attack_chain.action: Windows Explorer connects to a remote WebDAV share, displaying attacker-controlled files as local resources.
attack_chain.leads_to: User may execute or open malicious files, leading to malware infection.

attack_chain.action: Attacker removes the Windows Search protocol handler from the registry to cover tracks or prevent further use.
attack_chain.leads_to: Persistence/anti-forensics; final goal is malware execution and data exfiltration.

behavioral_signatures: HTML attachments with <meta http-equiv="refresh"> redirecting to search-ms: URIs
HTML links using search-ms: protocol with remote UNC paths
Unusual invocation of Windows Search from browser or email client context
Registry modifications deleting search-ms protocol handler
file_indicators: Zipped email attachments containing HTML files
References to \malicious-server\share or similar remote UNC paths
network_indicators: Outbound connections to remote WebDAV shares
Connections tunneled through Cloudflare or similar services
Unexpected SMB/WebDAV traffic following HTML file opening
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for email attachments containing HTML files with search-ms: URIs, especially those referencing remote UNC paths. Alert on <meta http-equiv="refresh"> tags that redirect to OS-level protocols. Detect registry modifications that remove protocol handlers. Correlate user actions opening HTML attachments with subsequent network connections to WebDAV/SMB shares. Flag any invocation of Windows Search from non-standard contexts such as browsers or email clients.
